idle · fork, waitpid and reap happen here
idle · a second app process, poked on purpose
poked, but no acknowledgement in this run
Five steps from fork() to verdict
mmap_lock belongs to the process, not to the thread
Android 14 and later: turn on Disable child process restrictions
The cap is not readable through any public API, so the probe makes the system enforce it and watches what happens.
Fork 66 children in the probe process. Each one only calls sleep() in a loop: no exec, no return to the JVM, so it stays a phantom process and cannot exit by itself.
Send an explicit broadcast to a second app process. AMS re-counts phantom processes when the app process set changes, so this poke is the trigger, not a formality.
Poll waitpid(pid, WNOHANG) per child. A child that reports back without us killing it was reaped by the system; that is the only evidence used.
Publish early. If nothing is reaped inside the 3 second settle window the verdict becomes no children reaped, and the probe keeps watching for another 60 seconds in case a late trim arrives.
Kill and reap the survivors, then let the probe process exit. Children carry PR_SET_PDEATHSIG, so a probe that dies takes its children with it.
fork() copies the page tables of the calling address space while holding its mmap_lock for the write side.

Every allocation on the UI thread takes the same mmap_lock for the read side, so it waits until the fork finishes. Compose allocates on every frame, which is why the same probe looks harmless in a View app and stalls an expressive UI.
On current hardware 66 forks cost around 300 milliseconds. Lower priority, batching and sleeps do not reduce that total; they only spread it over more frames.
mmap_lock belongs to the address space, not to a thread, so moving the fork to a background thread of the same process changes nothing.
Moved into :phantom, the probe has its own address space and its own lock. The UI process never touches mmap_lock, and the tap stays instant.
